What a Nil T2 Return Costs an Ontario Corporation

An Ontario corporation pays $300.00 plus HST per tax year for a nil T2 return, and because Ontario charges HST at 13 per cent the total is $339.00 per year. The price does not change with the age of the year, the size of the corporation or the number of shareholders, because a nil return carries the same preparation and the same CPA review whichever year it belongs to. Ontario corporate income tax is reported on the federal T2 rather than on a separate provincial return, so there is no second provincial filing fee the way an Alberta or Quebec corporation faces. What the fee does not cover is the Ontario annual return, which moved to the Ontario Business Registry in October 2021 and is filed separately.

What the Fee Includes

One nil T2 for one corporation for one tax year, including the T2 Short where the corporation qualifies, GIFI Schedules 100, 125 and 141 where they are required, Schedule 24 on a first return, Schedule 50 for every shareholder at 10 per cent or more, Schedule 8 and loss continuity, your Form T183CORP package with single-use secure e-signing, CPA review, electronic transmission by a registered EFILE electronic filer, one corrected transmission if the Agency rejects the first one, and your CRA confirmation emailed within 3 business days.

How It Works

  1. Type your corporation name. We fill the Business Number and incorporation date.
  2. Pick every tax year you have not filed and confirm the corporation had no activity in each of them.
  3. Complete the attestation and identity check, then pay $300.00 plus HST per tax year.
  4. Sign Form T183CORP. We transmit your return electronically.

Your CRA confirmation is emailed within 3 business days. Business days are Monday to Friday and exclude Ontario statutory holidays.

Filings This Does Not Cover

  • Your Ontario annual return. Since October 2021 it is filed through the Ontario Business Registry, and it is not covered by the $300.00 fee.
  • A federal Corporations Canada annual return, at $12.00, if your corporation is federally incorporated.
  • A nil GST/HST return or a nil payroll return.
  • RC145 closure of a GST/HST or payroll account.

We tell you which of these you still owe.

Unfiled T2 Returns and What They Do to an Ontario Corporation

An unfiled year never closes itself. For an Ontario corporation the exposure runs on two tracks at once, because the Canada Revenue Agency and the Ontario Business Registry keep separate records and neither one forgives the other. On the tax side the Agency can issue a demand to file and then assess the corporation arbitrarily on figures of its own. On the registry side a corporation that stops filing its Ontario annual returns under the Corporations Information Act can be dissolved by order of the Director. Ontario corporate income tax is reported on the federal T2, so catching up the T2 years is what clears the tax side, and it is the step that has to happen before a clearance certificate is possible.

What No Activity Means for an Ontario Corporation

No activity means no revenue, no expenses claimed, no payroll, no asset purchases and no inter-company transactions in the tax year. An Ontario corporation in that position still files a T2 within six months of its fiscal year-end, every year, until it is formally dissolved, and the return reports nil amounts rather than being skipped. The distinction that catches most Ontario owners is the balance sheet. A corporation can trade in no way at all and still hold share capital, a small cash balance, a shareholder loan or an unpaid incorporation cost, and any one of those makes GIFI Schedules 100, 125 and 141 required even though nothing happened during the year.

No Activity and the GIFI Schedules

A corporation inactive all year with nothing at all to report may omit GIFI Schedules 100, 125 and 141. Any share capital, cash, shareholder loan, incorporation cost or bank charge makes them required. This is the most common reason a return that looks nil is not filed correctly.

What Is Not No Activity

This service is for a corporation with no activity in the tax year. A corporation with investment income, rental income, or dividends paid or received is not nil.

Nil T2 Filing for an Ontario Numbered Corporation

A numbered corporation in Ontario carries a name of the form 1234567 Ontario Inc., assigned by the registry when the incorporators do not choose a name. It is an ordinary corporation in every respect that matters to the Canada Revenue Agency, which identifies it by business number rather than by name, so the T2 obligation and the due date are exactly those of a named corporation. Numbered corporations are over-represented among dormant Ontario companies, because many are incorporated to hold a single asset, to reserve a structure for later use, or as a shelf company that never began trading. None of those reasons removes the requirement to file every year until dissolution.

A numbered corporation is often set up for one purpose and then left alone. The return is still due for every year since incorporation.

When an Ontario Corporation Must File Its Nil T2

The deadline is six months after the fiscal year-end, and it is the same for an Ontario corporation as for any other resident corporation, because Ontario corporate income tax is reported on the federal T2 rather than on a separate provincial return with its own date. Where a due date falls on a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday recognised by the Canada Revenue Agency, a return received the next business day is on time. For Ontario corporations the business-day question matters in practice, because the statutory holidays that move a due date are the Ontario ones: Family Day in February and the August civic holiday both fall in months that are common fiscal year-ends.

Ontario Corporations Owned by Non-Residents

An Ontario corporation owned or controlled by non-residents is resident in Canada because it was incorporated here, so it files a T2 within six months of its fiscal year-end like any other Ontario corporation. Two things change. First, control by non-residents means the corporation is not a Canadian-controlled private corporation, which rules out the T2 Short and some of the simplifications that go with it. Second, the penalty position is different in the one way that matters most for a dormant company: a corporation owned by non-residents is exposed to a daily failure-to-file penalty whether or not it owes tax, so the usual comfort that a nil year costs nothing does not hold.

A true nil return carries no percentage late-filing penalty, because that penalty is a percentage of tax owing and the corporation owes $0.00. That last figure is the one to read twice. The percentage penalty is a percentage of tax owing and a nil year owes nothing, but the $25.00 a day applies to a non-resident-owned corporation regardless, to a maximum of $2,500.00 per year.
